extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of advertising history; historians and general readers interested in 18th–19th century newspaper advertisements
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and interpreting conventions, requirements, and rhetorical devices used in 18th–19th century newspaper advertisements (examples and commentary drawn from a history of advertising). Useful for studying ad form, tone, and stated conditions in historical classifieds and notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel/amusing invitation presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Set off invitations in a novel and amusing manner to ensure a large meeting and increase contributions (example: Cumberland Pacquet editor John Ware's style for 'bidden weddings').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor 'used to set off the invitation in a novel and amusing manner, which never failed to insure a large meeting, and frequently the contributions made on the occasion ... were of so much importance to the new-married couple that ... they were enabled to make so good a fund.' This illustrates using playful/clever wording and layout as a deliberate tactic to attract attendance and donations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bidding-wedding notice components
rubrics_metrics.description: Format and content conventions for a 'bidding' (public solicitation connected to marriage): date/location, announcement of intention to enter matrimonial state, invitation to a bidding at a named venue, solicitation of donations, promise to receive/acknowledge/repay, and explicit listing of family members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (Carmarthen, April 12, 1836) shows the conventional phrasing: statement of intent to marry, 'we are encouraged by our Friends to make a BIDDING on the occasion the same Day, at the Sign of the Angel ... the favour of your good and agreeable Company is most humbly solicited, and whatever donation you may be pleased to confer on us then, will be thankfully received, warmly acknowledged, and cheerfully repaid whenever called for.' The ad also lists related family members and requests return of prior gifts—demonstrating typical content and social/legal signals in such notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Servant (cook-housemaid) advertisement requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical explicit requirements in servant-help ads: strict age range, dual-role competence, and character specifications (sobriety, honesty, cleanliness), plus precise application instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'A COOK-HOUSEMAID, or HOUSEMAID-COOK ... The age ... must not be less than 25, nor more than 40 years; it is requisite that she should be equally excellent in the two capacities of Cook and Housemaid. Her character must be unexceptionable for sobriety, honesty and cleanliness.' The copy then clarifies undesirable interpretations of those terms (e.g., sobriety does not mean 'drinking deep without staggering'), warns impostors not to apply, and gives personal application hours and contact (1–3 o'clock to Mr Danvers). Shows ads demand both skill and moral/behavioural traits and provide procedural application details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chaperon advertisement conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed, often idiosyncratic attribute list required for a chaperon: extreme physical endurance, wakefulness, social-game skills, moderation of appetite, lack of personal attractiveness, freedom from matrimonial intent, and discriminating social judgment; exclusions by origin may be specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (satirical Morning Herald ad): 'must possess a constitution impervious to fatigue and heat, and be perfectly independent of sleep; fit at the mysteries of Whist and Cassino ... any personal charms ... will be deemed inadmissible; and she must be totally divested of matrimonial pretensions ... N.B. No Widow from Bath or Cheltenham will be treated with.' The ad both specifies requirements and uses comic/elitist social criteria, illustrating how employers advertised cultural expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: School-assistant advertisement criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements for school assistants in classifieds: respectable character and specific teaching scope (e.g., 'capable of TEACHING the CLASSICS as far as Homer and Virgil').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'TO SCHOOL ASSISTANTS.— Wanted, a respectable GENTLEMAN of good character, capable of TEACHING the CLASSICS as far as Homer and Virgil.' The subsequent anecdote (a letter joking about 'how far Homer and Virgil is from town') highlights the need for precise wording and how ambiguities could invite hoax replies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use (and decline) of poetical/verse advertisements
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical use of poetical or verse advertisements as a rhetorical device; by the 19th century they were common earlier but criticized as generally poor and largely obsolete due to space and faster news tempos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text states 'Poetical advertisements were not at all uncommon a hundred years ago ... They are, as a rule, infinitely bad,' and notes modern pressures ('the demand for space, and the steam-engine rate at which we live now') ended their use. Examples include Gavin Wilson's rhymed ad, a 'DRINKING SONG' for Lamplough's Pyretic Saline, and the 'SAVED' sandwich-man verse—useful exemplars and an explicit anti-pattern ('infinitely bad').

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale/transfer of charitable 'rounds' or rights (beggars' walks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ads selling or transferring proprietary rights to a begging route/crossing/walk typically state expected weekly takings, describe attendant assets (dog, staff), and require a premium payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'To be disposed of ... a Blind Man's WALK ... the comings-in between twenty-five and twenty-six shillings a week, with a dog well drilled, and a staff in good repair. A handsome premium will be expected.' This shows how even informal/social incomes were commodified and advertised with income estimates and asset descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classified goods/commodity condition specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Classified ads frequently specify exact physical/qualitative conditions for goods requested or offered (age, fitness, non-defect status).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an 1816 ad requesting '500 LIVE RATS' and explicitly adding 'The Rats must be full grown, and no cripples.' Demonstrates expectation of precise acceptance criteria for goods and the seller's/buyer's insistence on particular conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims, medals, guarantees, and exclusive agency as persuasive devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Product advertisements use claims of medals/awards (expositions), conditional guarantees ('NO HAIR NO MONEY'), and statements of exclusive agency/sole agent to build credibility and deter imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (from Handelsblad/American-Balsam): 'MEDAILLE of SILVER at New-York. MEDAILLE of GOLD at Paris, London and Berlin.' and the promise 'NO HAIR NO MONNEY' and 'THEOPHILE is sole agent for the Netherlands ...' These features function as trust signals and anti-counterfeit claims in product ads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of testimonials and published letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements often rely on published letters or testimonials (sometimes dramatic) as endorsements of product efficacy or service success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Gavin Wilson's advertisement is accompanied by 'The letter written by the sailor with the artificial hands to the printer of the Caledonian Mercury' (a testimonial written using his artificial hands). The page highlights how such letters were used to evidence product success and amuse readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inflated/exhaustive curriculum or capability lists as advertisement technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers (especially tutors/teachers) sometimes list an expansive, grandiose array of subjects and capabilities (often in pompous language) to attract pupils or customers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example Mr Hendrick's ad: promises instruction 'to teach the French language, Geography on the Principles of Astronomy, traversing the Globe by sea and land on the rudiments of a right angle, with a variety of pleasing Problems, attached to Manners, Customs, &c. of different Countries, Trade and Commerce; Phenomenons on Volcanos, Thunder, Sound, Lightning, &c.' Shows the tactic of overwhelming prospective clients with breadth and technical-sounding terms; the text also treats this as an instance of puffery/pomposity.
